commands.description: Evaluates the expression in the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, and prints its value as `nix-instantiate --eval` prints it. With an argument from `--arg` or `--argstr`, the value is called first, as `nix-instantiate --eval` calls it: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. Without one it is not called, and a function prints as `<LAMBDA>`; with `--aterm` it is called either way, as `nix-instantiate` calls it before it writes a derivation. A part of the value the evaluation never needed prints as `<CODE>`; with `--strict` the whole value is evaluated first. A relative path resolves against the file's directory, or for `--expr` and an `--arg` expression against the working directory. A `<name>` path, and a `<NAME>` argument, is looked up in the entries `--nix-path` adds, then `NIX_PATH`'s, then the `<nix/*>` expressions nova-nix ships with. An evaluation that writes to the store, as the fetchers do and, with `--read-write-mode`, `builtins.toFile` and `builtins.path` do, stops with an error at its first write to a store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed; one that writes nothing is not refused. With `NOVA_NIX_C_STATS` set to a file, an evaluation that succeeds writes to it a census of the memory its C data layer holds: the objects and bytes of each kind allocated, those its result, the root environment, the import cache and the search path still reach, and what finding them cost. With `NOVA_NIX_REGION_STATS` set to a file, it writes a census of regions: at the end of each force of a thunk, the bytes the force allocated and the bytes of them still reachable, and the most bytes collectors freeing at those points would have held.

commands.description: Evaluates the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, selects the attribute `-A` names when it is given, realises the output the `outputName` of the derivation that results names, the first of its outputs unless the expression selects another, building that derivation and every derivation it depends on as the output needs, and prints its path, as `nix-build` does; the derivation's other outputs are not asked for. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. A derivation whose outputs a substituter holds is downloaded instead of built, from the substituters `nix.conf` configures and the one `--substituter` adds, and only a path signed by a trusted key is accepted. The outputs of a derivation whose `allowSubstitutes` attribute is false are built instead, unless `always-allow-substitutes` is on. A substituter that fails stops the build unless `fallback` is on. With `--check` the derivation is checked as `nix-build --check` checks one: an output of its that is not valid is first downloaded from a substituter that holds it, the derivations it depends on are built or downloaded as ever, and then it is built again beside its outputs, never downloaded, and each output is compared with the one in the store. The rebuild changes nothing in the store and what it wrote is discarded; the downloads and builds before it add to the store as in any build. An output that comes out different fails the command with status 104, so a path a substituter supplied can be held to a build. With `keep-failed` on, a build that fails keeps its directory, under the store's `.nova-nix/builds`, until the derivation is next built, and names the directory its builder worked in on stderr, unless its builder is a builtin; and a check that finds an output different keeps that output's rebuild beside it as `PATH.check`, which nothing registers and the garbage collector removes, and names it in its error. The output is linked from `./result`, or from the path `--out-link` gives, with `-NAME` appended for an output `NAME` other than `out`, as `nix-build` links it, and the link is a root the garbage collector keeps; it replaces a link already there that points into the store, and anything else there fails the command. With `--no-out-link` nothing is linked. Where `sandbox` is on, as it is by default on Linux, a builder runs in a sandbox: it sees its inputs, the paths `sandbox-paths` names and its build directory, which on Linux it sees at `sandbox-build-dir`, and unless its derivation is fixed-output it reaches no network, which on Linux leaves it a loopback of its own; a system that cannot make the sandbox builds without it after a warning, or with `sandbox-fallback` off fails the build. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused before anything is evaluated.

commands.description: Evaluates the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, selects the attribute `-A` names when it is given, and starts `bash` with the environment the builder of the derivation that results has once its stdenv's setup has run, as `nix develop` does. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. The derivation's builder must be `bash`. A copy of it, named with `-env` after its name and with no checks on what its outputs refer to, is built in its place, with upstream's `get-env.sh` as its builder's script: it sources `$stdenv/setup` when `stdenv` is set, then writes the variables and functions bash holds to the copy's output, so the copy's path is the one `nix develop` builds. It reads the variables from the declare commands `declare -p` prints, which macOS's `/bin/bash`, bash 3.2, does not print, so a builder that is that bash captures none. What the derivation depends on is built or downloaded first, as `build` does, and a copy already built is not built again. The shell sets each variable and function again, but for those that belong to the shell running it, such as `HOME`, `TERM` and the temporary directories, with each output's path replaced by `outputs/NAME` under the working directory. It then puts the caller's `PATH` and `XDG_DATA_DIRS` after the captured ones, points `NIX_BUILD_TOP` and the temporary-directory variables at a fresh directory, and runs `shellHook`. Under structured attributes it reads `.attrs.sh` and `.attrs.json` from a temporary directory, which outlives the shell. An interactive shell reads `~/.bashrc` first and takes its prompt from the `bash-prompt` settings. With `--command` the command runs in place of an interactive shell, and with `--phase`, or a flag naming a phase, the phase runs through the setup's `runPhase`, or through `runHook` where it has none. The shell is `bash` found on the `PATH` of the environment it starts with, `/bin/bash` on macOS unless that `PATH` names another, with `SHELL` set to `bash` and `NIX_GCROOT` to the copy's output, which the garbage collector does not yet keep while the shell runs. That environment is the caller's, changed by `--ignore-env`, `--keep-env-var`, `--unset-env-var` and `--set-env-var`. nova-nix replaces itself with the shell, so the command exits with the shell's status. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused before anything is evaluated. On Windows the command is refused.

commands.description: Evaluates the file `PATH` names, or its `default.nix` when `PATH` is a directory, the file the search path finds for `<NAME>`, or the expression `--expr` gives, selects the attribute `-A` names when it is given, and reports what the closure of the derivation that results relies on. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. A closure bottoms out in fixed-output derivations, whose outputs are held to the hash their recipe states when a builtin fetches them or the closure builds them; one downloaded from a substituter is held to the content address its narinfo states, and to the narinfo's NarHash alone when it states none, as upstream holds one. First come those a build runs as builders, where a derivation's builder is inside one's output, or inside the tree a builtin such as `builtin:unpack` makes from it and any others; then those whose files hold prebuilt code, each with the files found; then those not fully read, each with what was not. Each says whether a builtin fetched it or the closure built it, and names any other with the same hash; a file of prebuilt code whose bytes are those of an input a build runs as a builder, such as a copy of a seed in a source archive, is named as that input. Then come how many hold no prebuilt code, the builders the closure does not contain, such as a program on the host, the builders in its input sources, the builtins nova-nix runs itself, and how many input sources its derivations take, store paths none of them builds. A fixed-output derivation whose builder is a builtin and which has no inputs is fetched first, or downloaded from a substituter, so that its bytes can be read; any other is only downloaded, with the paths it references, from a substituter that holds it, since making it would run its builder, and is read only when one does or the store already holds it. A fetch that fails stops the command, and so does a failed download of one that no builtin fetches. The scan finds prebuilt code by its header: a PE image, an ELF or Mach-O file, a COFF object, or an ar archive, whose members it does not read. It looks in a fetched file, in each file of a fetched tree, and in each file of a tar archive, plain or compressed with gzip, bzip2, xz or zstd, that one of those is; it does not open an archive inside another, and it reports a file in another archive format it knows, such as zip, as not read. It reports what the closure relies on, not whether any of it is safe. With `--json` it prints the same report as one JSON document, laid out over several lines when stdout is a terminal and on one otherwise, unless `--pretty` or `--no-pretty` says which: its `version`; `fixedOutputInputs`, keyed by output path, each with its `drvPath`, its `class`, `fetchedBy` or `builtBy`, `sameHash`, the builders inside it or its tree with their counts, `inStore`, and the `prebuiltCode` its scan found, each with its `kind`, `file`, `member`, `sha256` and the run-as-builder inputs it is the bytes of, and the files it did not read; `buildersOutsideClosure`, `buildersInInputSources` and `builtinBuilders`, each builder with how many derivations it builds; and `inputSources`, the paths themselves. In a store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, a closure with a fixed-output input is refused before any is fetched or read, and an evaluation that writes to the store stops at its first write, as `eval`'s does; a closure with no fixed-output input is reported there as anywhere.

commands.description: Copies the closure of each `PATH`, or with `--all` every valid path except derivations, to the binary cache at `URL`. A `PATH` is a store path, in full or as its base name; a derivation is refused, since a binary cache serves outputs. Paths the cache already holds are skipped, and every NAR is in place before any narinfo announces it. An `http://` or `https://` `URL` is a nova-cache server, which signs what it receives, and a narinfo is read back to check that the server signed it. A `file://` `URL` names a directory, which gets the layout upstream's `nix copy --to file://` writes, so that any web server can serve it and a substituter can read it through the same `URL`: `nix-cache-info`, a narinfo for each path, signed with the secret key in `--secret-key-file`, and the NARs under `nar/`. The key file is one `nix-store --generate-binary-cache-key` writes, and a substituter of the cache trusts its public key. It prints how many paths it pushed and how many the cache already held.

commands.description: Adds a package to a profile and switches the profile to a new generation that holds it, as `nix profile add` does. A `PATH` that is in the store, or a link that leads into it, as the `./result` a build links does, adds the store path it is in, which must be valid. Any other `PATH`, a `<NAME>` or `--expr` is evaluated as `build` evaluates its target, and its derivation built for the outputs it installs: the one the value selects when its `outputSpecified` is true, else those its `meta.outputsToInstall` names, else every output. Before each component of the `-A` path is selected from it, and once the path has selected it, the value is called as `nix-build` calls it, with the arguments from `--arg` and `--argstr` or with none: a set with `__functor` stands for what its functor returns given the set, which is called in turn; a function with a set pattern is called with every argument when it takes `...` and otherwise with those its formals name, its defaults filling the rest, and a formal with neither an argument nor a default fails the command; any other value is left as it is. The package is named after the names of its paths without their versions, with `-1`, `-2` and on appended to a name the profile already holds, and has the priority `--priority` gives, 5 unless it gives another. Where two packages hold a file at one path, the profile links the one with the lower number, and two with one number fail the command, which names both files and the commands that would resolve it. A profile is a link to one of its generations, `PROFILE-1-link`, `PROFILE-2-link` and on beside it, each a store path holding the packages' files linked into one tree and a `manifest.json` that lists the packages, and each a root the garbage collector keeps. The default profile is `profiles/profile` in the state directory, which is `$NIX_STATE_HOME`, else `$XDG_STATE_HOME/nix`, else `~/.local/state/nix`, or on Windows `nix\state` in the Local AppData folder; `~/.nix-profile`, or with `use-xdg-base-directories` on `profile` in the state directory, links to it, and both are made when they are missing, whichever profile `--profile` names. A profile whose current generation is outside the store, as one upstream Nix keeps in `/nix/store` is while nova-nix uses another store, is refused. A change that finds the profile changed by another command since it began starts again. On Windows each link is a symlink, which needs Developer Mode or an elevated shell. A store directory that upstream Nix's database also manages, such as `/nix/store` where upstream Nix is installed, is refused before anything is evaluated.

commands.description: Deletes every generation of a profile but its current one, as `nix profile wipe-history` does, saying `removing profile version N` for each, so that none can be rolled back to; the next `store gc` drops their roots and deletes what only they kept. With `--older-than Nd`, `N` a whole number of days from 1, it deletes only the generations made more than `N` days ago, but the newest of them, which the profile held then, and never the current one; one made since then that is numbered below the newest of them is kept, with a warning. A generation was made when its link was. With `--dry-run` it says `would remove profile version N` for each and deletes nothing. A profile with no current generation keeps none for being current. A profile's generations are `PROFILE-1-link`, `PROFILE-2-link` and on beside it, and its current one is the one its link names by that bare name, as a switch writes it; a link naming anything else, an absolute path included, names no current generation. The default profile and its link are made when they are missing, and a profile whose current generation is outside the store is refused, as for every profile command. On Windows each link is a symlink, which needs Developer Mode or an elevated shell.

configuration.description: `nix.conf` is read in upstream's order: `$NIX_CONF_DIR/nix.conf`, where `NIX_CONF_DIR` defaults to `/etc/nix`, or `%ProgramData%\nix` on Windows; the XDG `nix/nix.conf` files, the config home's in `$NIX_CONFIG_HOME` when that is set, or `$NIX_USER_CONF_FILES`; then `$NIX_CONFIG`. A later source replaces an earlier one's value, an `extra-` prefix on a list setting adds to it instead, and a flag adds to whatever they configure: an entry to a list, or a Boolean moved from its default, which a flag cannot move back.

global.description: nova-nix evaluates Nix expressions, builds derivations, starts shells with a derivation's build environment, reports what a derivation's closure relies on, pushes store paths to a binary cache, keeps profiles of packages and maintains its store, one command per invocation, and reads its settings from `nix.conf` as upstream Nix does. Each command takes the flags listed with it, after the command's name. A command exits with status 0 when it succeeds, and with status 1 when it fails, after saying why on stderr; `build --check` has another status, 104, for an output that differs, and `develop`, once its shell has started, exits with the shell's.
